projectBriefConcise: Two Storey Side Extension on the corner side with a First Floor Rear Projection, Single Storey Rear Extension across the full width of the house replacing the Existing Conservatory to form an open plan Kitchen and Dining Room, conversion of the Existing Garage, a remodelled Entrance Hall and Staircase, a wider Lounge, and a new Boundary Fence along the road.
projectBriefFull:
## Thank You
Thank you for your hospitality on Monday 5ᵗʰ October. You went to real effort with the cups of tea and the beautiful South Indian food, and it made the day an absolute treat for me. I enjoyed sitting down with you and working through the ideas together. Thank you also to Dr Deepak for recommending me.

## Project Overview And Goals
Your home is a detached, volume-built house from the 1990s or early 2000s, on a corner plot. Houses of that age were divided into far more separate rooms than people want today, and yours shows it: a dark, corridor-like hallway, a kitchen too small and too dark for modern family life, and a garage and conservatory that, as you put it, are dead space for half the year. There is little about the house that needs protecting, which leaves room to change it substantially.

From your notes and our day on site, the aims are:

- more space, with en-suites to the main bedrooms;
- a large, bright, open plan kitchen and dining room you can use all year round;
- a lounge kept separate from the kitchen, and made wider;
- the garage and utility turned into rooms and storage you actually use;
- much better storage throughout.

We sat together and sketched some very early options. Nothing is set in stone. The concept design stage will settle every room and give you a 3D model in TrueVision that you can walk around before anything is drawn for planning.

## Your Daughter's Suite
It was clear how much you want your daughter to have a real say. When she came home at the end of the day, you made sure she was part of the conversation. I'd like to keep it that way: she should be at the concept review meeting, so the decisions about her room are hers too.

Her brief, as I have it:

- space for a king-size bed;
- a walk-in wardrobe with a dressing area and a dressing table;
- an en-suite shower room of her own;
- in effect, her own hotel suite;
- and the hot tub she would like in the garden, reached through the new doors from the kitchen.

## The Side Boundary
Where your side boundary runs has concerned you from the start, and it decides how much can be built on the corner side.

The hedge along the road is in the wrong place. It angles in towards the house and steps back by the width of the side gate, so part of your garden looks like council verge. The developer probably planted it there to save on fencing. While I was with you, you bought your title plan from HM Land Registry, and we compared it with the MapServe preview of the Ordnance Survey data. The two agree: the boundary runs in a much straighter line along the road, carrying on the line of your existing boundary further down the garden. Beside the house it is more than two metres from the side wall, possibly three. The boundary is not doglegged in after all.

The plan:

- I buy the Ordnance Survey data and align it with your title plan and with the LiDAR scan from the survey;
- the hedge comes out, and a new fence goes up on the boundary, continuing the line of your existing boundary;
- the side extension runs from the existing side wall of the house to about 200 mm short of the new fence: as far as planning permission allows, with room left to clear leaves and debris.

A fence over one metre high next to a road needs planning permission, so the new fence will be part of the planning application.

One caution. Title plans show general boundaries, not the exact legal line, so my drawings will show the best fit of your title plan and the Ordnance Survey data to the scan. Please be happy with the line before the hedge comes out. The Building Surveying terms set this out.

## Proposed Ground Floor Alterations
- **Kitchen and dining.** The conservatory comes down and a single storey extension runs 3 metres into the garden across the full width of the back of the house. Kitchen, dining and the old conservatory space become one open plan room you can use all year, with a large island in the middle under a roof light. You mentioned a German-style kitchen for storage, and a straight or L-shaped layout; the 3D model is the place to decide.
- **Light.** The kitchen is dark now, and doubling its depth would make the middle darker still. A roof light over the island and multi-folding doors across the back, with a clear sightline to the garden, will more than make up for it. Your ground floor is too dark and closed-in, as is typical of houses of this age, so I want to go further than simply making up the difference.
- **Heating.** In a room this size, underfloor heating is worth considering: no radiators taking up wall space, and no cold spots.
- **Lounge.** Kept separate from the kitchen, as you want, and made about a metre wider by taking in part of the current hallway.
- **Hallway and stairs.** The hallway becomes a brighter, more open entrance rather than a dark corridor. The stairs may be turned round or reworked to make room for the wider lounge. Floating stairs, if the budget allows, and better use of the space under the stairs, where the WC and shoe rack are, will both be looked at.
- **Porch.** You'd like a bigger porch with a higher ceiling, without changing the layout. I'll look at this in the concept.
- **Garage, utility and the new side space.** The garage, the converted garage room, the utility and the ground floor of the side extension become new rooms. Your notes mention a guest room with an en-suite or a day bed, a media room, space for table tennis or a treadmill, a bigger utility, a wet room and a storeroom. This part wasn't resolved on the day, so I'll go through your requirements again at the start of the concept stage and design it properly.
- **Your dog.** You'd like somewhere to keep your golden retriever's things so the house smells less, perhaps by the utility or in the garden. This will be part of the concept.

## Proposed First Floor Alterations
- **Side extension.** A two storey extension on the corner side, from the existing side wall out towards the new fence, with a first floor projection off its back into the garden. The room above the garage loses its dormer, as Sukhi suggested, and becomes a wider room with better space.
- **Bedrooms and bathrooms.** We sketched two directions: every bedroom with an en-suite and no family bathroom, or a family bathroom with en-suites to the larger bedrooms. Where we left it: three main bedrooms with en-suites, and one or two bedrooms sharing a family bathroom. The family bathroom sits on the landing at the top of the stairs, and you are happy to lose it if every room has an en-suite.
- **Your daughter's suite**, as above.
- **Your own bedroom.** Its bathroom grows by taking in the storage area, as you described. I've assumed you'd like your bedroom to the same standard as your daughter's; tell me if not.
- **The study** could stay a study with a sofa bed, become an office, or become a bedroom. We'll decide once you can see the layout.

The side extension and the existing first floor have room for all of this, plus an additional en-suite bedroom. Which room goes where will be settled at concept stage.

## Why The First Floor Goes On The Corner Side
Your notes suggest extending your daughter's room and the study back over the new kitchen, and on the day we also looked at taking the roof back across the full width of the house. I advised against both, and we agreed to drop them:

- **Your neighbour.** A first floor across the back of the house would sit close to your neighbour, take light from their rear windows and garden, and overlook them. The council must protect neighbours' light and privacy, and this is the kind of scheme it refuses.
- **Cost.** Taking the roof back would need a crown roof, replacing the whole roof of the house and reworking your solar panels. It would become very expensive.
- **The planning case.** There are no neighbours on the corner side. Putting the extra first floor space there, as a projection off the back of the side extension, lets the Design and Access Statement show the council that every measure has been taken to protect your neighbour's light and privacy.

I've been in this position many times, and this is the best option. Anything else, the planners will send back for a redesign or, if they are short of time, simply refuse. Each new application costs another council fee, currently £548, plus months of delay. We really don't want to be doing that.

## Construction Budget
On the day we worked out a rough budget together, running the areas through an AI tool in front of you so you could see how the figures were reached:

- **Ground floor extension.** About 25 m² at £2,500 per m²: £62,500.
- **First floor extension.** About 30 m² at £2,500 per m²: £75,000.
- **Total.** About 55 m²: £137,500 plus VAT, or £165,000 including VAT at 20%.

For everything you're looking to do, I'd expect the build to cost between about £130,000 and £160,000 plus VAT. The lower figure assumes the cheapest option for everything, and I doubt Sukhi Home Solutions would price it that low. These are rough figures from the day. I'll reconfirm the areas with you as the concept takes shape, and Sukhi Home Solutions will price the build properly once it's drawn.

## My Fee
The AI estimate on the day put the design fees at about £3,600 to £4,000. Like most architects, I set my fee in proportion to the value of the build, and from a build value of about £150,000 we arrived at £3,400.

I gave you that figure without mentioning VAT, which I should have done. VAT at 20% has to be charged, and every invoice will show it. As the oversight was mine, I'm splitting the difference: I'm covering half the VAT, so you pay £3,740 in total rather than £4,080. The quotation shows this as a Goodwill Gesture.

The fee is based on the areas and scope we agreed on site. If, before I start the design, the floor area turns out very different or the scheme becomes simpler, I'll adjust the fee fairly. Once a design has been drawn, later reductions don't reduce the fee.

## What Happens Next
- **Survey.** A return visit to scan the whole house, inside and out, with LiDAR, and the roof and plot by drone, on a date we agree. Before the visit, please read "Preparing for Your Survey" in the Building Surveying contract on this portal. It covers mirrors, curtains, window sills, loft access and the rest.
- **Existing model.** I build a 3D model of the house and plot from the scan.
- **Concept design.** I design the scheme and publish it in TrueVision, so you can walk around it in 3D.
- **Review meeting.** We go through it together, with your daughter, and agree any changes.
- **Planning drawings.** Once you approve the concept, I produce the planning drawings and CGIs.
- **Submission.** I submit a householder planning application to Rushcliffe Borough Council. Once the application is validated, the council aims to decide within eight weeks, though it often extends that.

As a rough guide, expect the concept about four to six weeks after the survey, and the planning drawings about four weeks after you approve the concept.

## Planning And Building Regulations
- **Submission only.** I prepare the drawings and forms and submit the application. Once the council confirms it is valid, my role as agent ends and the application is yours to run: correspondence with the planning officer, any further reports, chasing and being chased. If I'm asked to deal with it after that, I charge £50 per hour.
- **Managed planning application.** The quotation offers this at £500: I'd handle every call and email with the council for you. I always offer it, but on this job I don't think it's good value, and I wouldn't take it if I were you.
- **Design and Access Statement.** Optional, at £200. It's where the written case is made for the side extension and for protecting your neighbour. It will be to the same standard as the statement I showed you, which cost £400; yours is about 70% of the work, because your house isn't in the Green Belt.
- **Third-party fees.** The council's application fee is currently £548, paid through me before submission. Submitting through the national Planning Portal adds a £149 service charge; Rushcliffe accepts applications by email, so that one is optional. The Ordnance Survey data is about £40.
- **Building regulations.** Sukhi Home Solutions will take on everything after planning: the technical design, the specification, structural engineering, Building Control, and the legal duties under the Building Safety Act, which have to sit with someone. That won't be me. I always offer a Building Regulations package (£3,000 on the quotation), but with Sukhi Home Solutions taking this on, you won't need it.

## Please Check: Loft Conversions
This appointment does not include a loft conversion. A loft conversion is specialist engineering work that needs a specialist roof survey, and it hasn't been priced. I wouldn't advise one here. There are a few on your estate, and loft conversions are notoriously harder to get through than what you're planning. Engineered roof structures are very expensive, and loft conversions are usually a last resort where space is at a premium. Your side garden isn't ground you'd use as a proper garden, so building on it is the better option.

If you think you might want to convert the loft, please tell me before you sign. It changes the survey, the design and the price.
